title: Bara Brith
subtitle: Welsh fruit bread steeped in tea
excerpt: Dried fruit soaked overnight in strong tea, folded into a spiced bread dough with brown sugar and an egg. Baked until dark and dense, then sliced and buttered. The definitive Welsh bake.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bara brith means 'speckled bread' in Welsh, referring to the dried fruit distributed through the dough. There are two distinct versions: a yeasted bread version, which is lighter and more traditionally Welsh, and the easier no-yeast version made with self-raising flour, which is now the most commonly made. Both require soaking the dried fruit in tea, which plumps the fruit, flavours it, and provides the liquid for the batter. The no-yeast version is essentially a tea loaf and requires no kneading or proving. It keeps extremely well and improves over three to four days as the fruit continues to soften.

content.text: The fruit must be soaked overnight: this is not optional. The soaked fruit will be plump and the tea will have been mostly absorbed, leaving behind a concentrated, tannic liquid. Use a strong black tea with no milk. The batter will be thick and sticky. The loaf takes longer to bake than most cakes: a skewer in the centre should come out completely clean.

items.preparation: made into 300 ml strong black tea, cooled

content.text: The night before: combine the dried fruit, sugar, and hot tea in a large bowl. Stir, cover, and leave to soak overnight at room temperature.
Heat the oven to 160 C / fan 140 C / gas 3. Grease and line a 900 g loaf tin. Stir the beaten egg and mixed spice into the soaked fruit. Sift in the flour and fold together until just combined.
Spoon into the prepared tin. Bake for 1 hour 30 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. If the top colours too quickly, cover loosely with foil after 1 hour.
Brush the warm loaf with marmalade for a glossy finish. Cool in the tin for 20 minutes, then turn out and cool completely on a rack. Slice and serve with plenty of cold butter.
